###### Abstract

Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations
research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without
prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks commonly begin with
self-contained problem descriptions or predefined optimization tasks,
leaving the work of translating original business materials into
professionally validated solutions underrepresented. We introduce
OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial
scenarios drawn from paid OR engagements totaling \$3.68 million in
project value. It preserves original requirements, input data,
deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification.
To evaluate information acquisition throughout optimization, we further
introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business
facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks
feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert
solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction.
Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality
across instances, assigning zero credit to infeasible deliveries. Across
11 frontier LLMs evaluated with coding-agent harnesses, several exceed
the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches
its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39%
strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1.
Client information acquisition extends beyond initial clarification into
solution development and validation, with some later stages exhibiting
higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis
identifies failures spanning formulation and implementation, while
task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45%
across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained
information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and
evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.

## 1 Introduction

Operations research (OR) supports high-value decisions across
manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, retail, and many other domains.
Deploying an OR system, however, requires experts to transform
incomplete business materials into an executable decision process
through requirement elicitation, problem formulation, solution strategy
selection, and solver implementation. Gurobi’s State of Mathematical
Optimization Report 2024 reports that 82% of survey respondents hold a
master’s or doctoral degree ([Gurobi Optimization, 2024](#bib.bib16)).
We ask whether large language model (LLM) agents can carry out this
work.

Recent work has explored LLMs for OR ([Ramamonjison et al.,
2023](#bib.bib38); [Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib49); [Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib29); [AhmadiTeshnizi
et al., 2024](#bib.bib2); [Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib8); [Sun et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)), with newer benchmarks
extending evaluation to multi-stage agent workflows ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52); [Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib25)). However, three
important gaps remain in evaluating whether LLMs can take on the work of
OR experts in real-world engagements. Gap 1: Task Complexity and
Practical Relevance. Benchmarks built from academic, synthetic, or
reconstructed tasks may not capture the operational complexity and
practical demands of real client engagements, limiting what their
results reveal about LLMs’ ability to perform professional OR work. Gap
2: Information Acquisition. Evaluations that provide the full task
context omit the work required to establish that context, a limitation
explicitly acknowledged by GDPval ([Patwardhan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36)). In real OR engagements, practitioners must identify
missing client-held information, ask targeted questions, and integrate
the answers throughout problem solving. Gap 3: Limited Grounding in
Professional Delivery. Professional OR capability requires a reference
grounded in the solution quality achieved by experts in real client
engagements, alongside correctness checks and algorithmic baselines.
Evaluation-specific references can validate task criteria, whereas
client-accepted expert deliveries anchor the comparison in outcomes that
satisfied real client requirements.

![Refer to caption](2610.24087v1/or_license_motivation.png)

Figure 1: Three gaps and corresponding improvements in OR-License. Each
column links an evaluation gap (top) to its improvement (bottom). The
client dialogue is illustrative.

As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"),
to address these gaps, we introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark
built from real-world OR engagements. The name reflects our focus on the
skills required in professional OR practice. OR-License comprises three
core improvements: First, we ground evaluation in original paid
industrial OR engagements, preserving realistic requirements, artifacts,
and ambiguity after de-identification. Second, we introduce ORSim, which
lets agents acquire client-side business information throughout the
workflow while maintaining a boundary between customer knowledge and OR
expertise. Third, we evaluate agents against original expert solutions
that were accepted by clients before benchmark construction, providing a
realistic reference for professional-quality delivery.

We use OR-License to investigate three research questions:

RQ1: How do LLM agents compare with OR experts in feasibility and
objective quality, and how consistently do they complete
evidence-grounded investigations?

RQ2: When do agents acquire client information across the OR workflow,
and how does it contribute to confirmed issue resolution?

RQ3: What failure patterns emerge when agents translate business
requirements into executable OR solutions, and what capability gaps do
they reveal?

The contributions of this work are threefold:

- •
  A dataset grounded in paid industrial OR engagements. We curate and
  release 31 instances across 10 industries, derived from commissioned
  OR projects representing \$3.68 million in total project value
  (Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Data Curation ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")).
- •
  An end-to-end evaluation framework for LLM agents as OR practitioners.
  We formalize the OR workflow from requirement elicitation to
  executable decision making and introduce ORSim, a controlled client
  simulator that provides business facts throughout formulation,
  solving, and refinement without supplying OR expertise. We integrate
  this interaction with coding-agent harnesses and hidden
  post-submission evaluation of feasibility and expert-relative solution
  quality
  (Sections [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Task Definition ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
  and [4](#S4 "4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")).
- •
  Deployment-oriented metrics and trajectory analysis. We introduce
  Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ), averaging expert-relative quality
  with zero credit for infeasible deliveries, and a Reliability–Quality
  Profile. Across eleven frontier LLMs, we analyze client information
  acquisition, failure patterns, and linked cycles of hypothesis
  formation, experimentation, and revision to relate observed inquiry to
  delivery performance
  (Sections [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
  and [4](#S4 "4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")).

## 2 Related Work

##### LLMs for Operations Research.

OptiMUS uses a modular agent for mathematical formulation, solver-code
generation, and execution-based revision ([AhmadiTeshnizi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2)). ORLM, ReSocratic, and OptMATH improve optimization
modeling through specialized training and data synthesis ([Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib49); [Lu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib29)), while ARS generates constraint-aware heuristic code
for vehicle-routing variants ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)). Many
existing evaluations begin with self-contained problem descriptions or
predefined optimization tasks ([Ramamonjison et al., 2023](#bib.bib38);
[Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib49); [Lu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)). OR-Space and ORAgentBench extend evaluation
to multi-file executable environments and multi-stage workflows ([Zhou
et al., 2026](#bib.bib52); [Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib25)). OR-License
builds on this direction using original materials from paid industrial
engagements, preserving their requirements, data formats, ambiguity,
terminology, and information boundaries after de-identification. Agents
can query ORSim throughout formulation, solving, and refinement, making
client interaction part of building the executable solution.

##### Benchmarking LLMs for Professional Work.

Recent benchmarks such as GDPval, APEX-Agents, and AgencyBench evaluate
economically valuable deliverables and sustained execution across
professional tasks and realistic scenarios ([Patwardhan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36); [Vidgen et al., 2026](#bib.bib46); [Li et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib27)). OR-License specializes this direction to OR:
executable submissions are checked for feasibility against original
client requirements, and objective quality is assessed relative to
original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark
construction.
Table [8](#A6.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix F Extended Comparison with Related Benchmarks ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
summarizes the comparison.

## 3 Benchmark Construction

In this section, we define the tasks in OR-License and describe data
curation, client interaction through ORSim, and the evaluation protocol.
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
provides an overview.

![Refer to caption](2610.24087v1/or_license_framework.png)

Figure 2: The OR-License evaluation framework. Experts curate tasks and
reference solutions from real-world OR projects. Agents may query ORSim
throughout problem solving. Final submissions undergo hidden evaluation
of feasibility and expert-relative solution quality.

### 3.1 Task Definition

An OR-License scenario $`s`$ corresponds to an industry and comprises a
set of OR instances $`\mathcal{I}_{s}`$. Each instance
$`i\in\mathcal{I}_{s}`$ defines a concrete OR task with its own decision
structure, business rules, objective, and official test cases
$`c\in\mathcal{C}_{i}`$. For each case $`c`$, let $`\mathcal{Y}_{i,c}`$
denote the decision space,
$`f_{i,c}:\mathcal{Y}_{i,c}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}`$ the objective
function, and $`\mathrm{verifier}_{i,c}`$ a hidden programmatic checker
that validates a submitted decision against the task-specific hard
constraints and required relationships among decision variables. The
underlying optimization problem is

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{i,c}}\;\sigma_{i}f_{i,c}(y)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\mathrm{verifier}_{i,c}(y)=\text{pass},\qquad\sigma_{i}\in\{+1,-1\},
``` |  |

where $`\sigma_{i}=+1`$ for maximization and $`\sigma_{i}=-1`$ for
minimization.

For each instance, the agent receives an initial business brief and all
task input files, and may query ORSim for additional client-held
business facts throughout formulation, solving, and refinement. It then
produces an executable decision
$`\widehat{y}_{i,c}\in\mathcal{Y}_{i,c}`$ for each test case $`c`$.
OR-License evaluates the feasibility of $`\widehat{y}_{i,c}`$ through
$`\mathrm{verifier}_{i,c}(\widehat{y}_{i,c})`$ and its objective quality
through $`f_{i,c}(\widehat{y}_{i,c})`$, which is independently
recomputed from the agent’s submitted decision.

### 3.2 Data Curation

We curated 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from commissioned
OR engagements. Experts with at least three years of professional OR
experience de-identified the original requirements, input data, and
deliverable formats while preserving the information boundary presented
to the agent. They prepared the initial business brief and annotated the
client-held facts that could be acquired through ORSim. Detailed
recruitment criteria and curation procedures are provided in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Dataset Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

Each instance provides the agent with the de-identified input files and
initial brief. Hidden instance-specific verifiers and objective
functions evaluate submitted decisions against the original operational
requirements, while original expert solutions accepted by the clients
provide the reference deliveries. Experts reviewed the consistency among
the original project requirements, agent-facing materials, hidden
evaluators, and reference solutions. The source engagements represent
\$3.68 million in total project value; problem sizes and additional
engagement statistics are reported in
Appendices [G](#A7 "Appendix G Dataset Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
and [G.3](#A7.SS3 "G.3 Problem Sizes ‣ Appendix G Dataset Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Data Curation ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
summarizes these engagement statistics.

### 3.3 ORSim

Real-world OR requirements are often incomplete at the start of a
project and may require clarification during formulation, solving, and
refinement. We therefore introduce ORSim, a controlled
client-interaction environment that exposes scenario-grounded client
facts throughout the episode while withholding OR expertise. Each
instance begins with an initial business brief and an expert-reviewed
catalog of client facts. The evaluated agent cannot inspect this catalog
or the hidden evaluator. Only eligible client-owned facts can be
disclosed, while problem formulation, algorithm selection, and solver
implementation remain the agent’s responsibility. Each query can
disclose at most three non-brief facts.

For each question, a simulator-side LLM selects relevant entries from
the closed fact catalog. A deterministic controller validates the
selection and enforces the ownership, visibility, and per-query
disclosure rules before passing the authorized text to a response-only
LLM for natural-language rendering. The selector and responder do not
determine which information may be disclosed. This separation allows
flexible semantic matching and language generation while keeping the
information boundary programmatic. We evaluate ORSim with
expert-annotated reliability tests; the complete schema, selector
variants, disclosure rules, and evaluation protocol are provided in
Appendix §[C](#A3 "Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

### 3.4 Metrics

A deployable OR solution must satisfy every operational constraint and
attain a competitive objective value. These requirements are
hierarchical because solution quality has operational meaning only after
feasibility is established. We therefore report instance-level
feasibility, expert-relative quality, and a feasibility-gated overall
score.

##### Strict Feasibility.

For $`N`$ instances indexed by $`i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}`$, let
$`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ be the official test cases of instance $`i`$, and
let $`\widehat{y}_{i,c}`$ be the final submitted output for case $`c`$.
An instance is feasible only if every official case passes its hidden
verifier:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle F_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\forall c\in\mathcal{C}_{i},\;\mathrm{verifier}_{i,c}(\widehat{y}_{i,c})=\mathrm{pass}\right],`$ |  | (1) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Feas}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}F_{i}.`$ |  |  |

Let $`\mathcal{F}=\{i:F_{i}=1\}`$ and $`K=|\mathcal{F}|`$.

##### Expert-Relative Quality.

For each $`i\in\mathcal{F}`$, let $`J_{i}^{\mathrm{agent}}`$ and
$`J_{i}^{\mathrm{expert}}`$ use the same fixed instance aggregation, and
define $`\widetilde{J}_{i}^{(\cdot)}=T_{i}(J_{i}^{(\cdot)})>0`$. The
instance-specific transformation $`T_{i}`$ is strictly increasing and
applied identically to the system and expert objectives. We define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{i}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\widetilde{J}_{i}^{\mathrm{expert}}}{\widetilde{J}_{i}^{\mathrm{agent}}},&\text{if instance $i$ is a minimization problem},\\[8.0pt]
\dfrac{\widetilde{J}_{i}^{\mathrm{agent}}}{\widetilde{J}_{i}^{\mathrm{expert}}},&\text{if instance $i$ is a maximization problem}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (2) |

Here $`Q_{i}=1`$ matches the expert objective, with larger values
indicating better solutions. Conditional quality is
$`Q_{\mathrm{feas}}=K^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}Q_{i}`$, reported as N/A
when $`K=0`$.
Appendix §[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Objective Normalization and Expert-Relative Quality ‣ Appendix A Metric Definitions and Analysis ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
specifies the objective-scale normalization and edge-case conventions.

##### Deployment-Adjusted Quality.

We gate solution quality by setting $`Z_{i}=Q_{i}`$ for $`F_{i}=1`$ and
$`Z_{i}=0`$ otherwise. The benchmark-level *Deployment-Adjusted Quality*
(DAQ) is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\boxed{\begin{aligned} \mathrm{DAQ}&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}Q_{i}\\
&=\mathrm{Feas}\,Q_{\mathrm{feas}}\qquad(K>0).\end{aligned}}
``` |  | (3) |

If $`K=0`$, $`\mathrm{DAQ}=0`$. The expert reference has
$`\mathrm{DAQ}=1`$.

##### Reliability-Quality Profile.

DAQ is the parameter-free primary metric. To expose how rankings change
as evaluation becomes more sensitive to low instance scores, we define
the power-mean family ([Hardy et al., 1952](#bib.bib17))

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\boxed{\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha}=\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}^{1/\alpha}\right)^{\alpha}}.
``` |  | (4) |

$`\mathrm{Feas}`$, DAQ, and $`\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha}`$ macro-average over
instances, assigning each instance weight $`1/N`$ regardless of its
number of official cases. Here $`\mathrm{DAQ}_{1}=\mathrm{DAQ}`$, and
$`\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha}`$ is monotonically nonincreasing in $`\alpha`$.
Larger $`\alpha`$ values penalize low instance-level scores, including
incomplete and uneven delivery, more strongly.
Appendix §[A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Reliability-Quality Profile ‣ Appendix A Metric Definitions and Analysis ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
gives the decomposition, monotonicity argument, and compensation
analysis.

We use DAQ as the primary score and evaluate the reliability-quality
profile at $`\alpha\in\{1.0,1.1,\ldots,3.0\}`$, a pre-specified grid of
21 values with step size $`0.1`$.

### 3.5 Trajectory Analysis Methodology

Final-delivery scores do not reveal how agents acquire information,
repair errors, or conduct evidence-linked revisions. We therefore
manually annotate three observable dimensions of each retained
trajectory using task materials, interaction logs, execution feedback,
and final artifacts. The complete coding and aggregation protocol is
given in
Appendix §[B](#A2 "Appendix B Trajectory Analysis Protocol ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

For client information acquisition, we assign each ask action to one of
six OR workflow stages: before solver code (S1), before solver feedback
(S2), before the first candidate (S3), before a complete candidate (S4),
before the self-check passes (S5), and before final submission (S6). We
also record whether the agent asks again after solving feedback when
another decision opportunity remains.

For scientific inquiry, we annotate research opportunities:
consequential uncertainties visible to the agent and potentially
reducible through investigation. For each opportunity, we identify a
testable hypothesis (H), a mechanistic explanation (C), an executed
diagnostic experiment (A), evidence interpretation (E), and an
evidence-grounded update (U). A complete HCAEU chain links these
behaviors within the same issue and branch: H and C precede A, the
experimental result informs E, and E leads to U. We report chain
completion and, among opportunities with a complete chain, stage quality
based on a three-level rubric. The rubric and aggregation rules are
given in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Trajectory Analysis Protocol ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

For trajectory-level error analysis, we identify confirmed error events
from the agent trajectory and final artifact and classify each event by
its point of origin. We use eight categories: problem understanding
(UND), data and parameter mapping (DATA), decision representation (DEC),
static constraints (CON), dynamic and state transitions (DYN),
uncertainty and information structure (UNC), objective and preference
formulation (OBJ), and implementation and delivery (IMP). Because a
trajectory may contain multiple error events, category profiles are
computed at the event level, with infeasible rates reported separately.

## 4 Evaluation

We evaluate eleven frontier models on the three research questions
introduced in
Section [1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"),
with five runs per model–task pair. Feasibility and DAQ first average
the five runs within each task, then weight the 31 task means equally.
Their reported spreads are the arithmetic means of the within-task
sample standard deviations; conditional quality and its spread divide
the DAQ mean and spread by the observed mean feasibility. These spreads
describe within-task variation, not standard errors of the benchmark
mean. Reliability–quality profiles apply the same task-equal averaging
to $`Z^{1/\alpha}`$ before raising the result to $`\alpha`$.

We further analyze agents’ solution techniques, objective handling, and
problem-structure exploitation in comparison with expert reference
solutions in
Appendix §[E](#A5 "Appendix E Solution Strategies and Optimization-Structure Exploitation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

The complete model list, prompt templates, evaluation settings, and the
average cost of each agent are provided in
Appendix §[D](#A4 "Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

##### Execution setup.

We use Claude Code as the primary evaluation harness and expose ORSim
through the Bash command ask. This provides a common shell-based
interface for model execution while keeping client interaction within
the benchmark protocol. An additional Codex harness comparison is
reported in
Appendix [D.7](#A4.SS7 "D.7 Harness Ablation ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").
Complete model versions, execution budgets, prompts, and
instance-specific settings are provided in
Appendices [D](#A4 "Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
and [G](#A7 "Appendix G Dataset Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

### 4.1 RQ1: Cross-Model Comparison and Performance Against Human Experts

##### Metric-based results.

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
shows that the models differ more in whether they complete a feasible
delivery than in their conditional objective quality. Feasibility spans
$`43.23`$ percentage points, from $`45.16\%`$ for Hy3 to $`88.39\%`$ for
Grok 4.6, whereas conditional quality spans only $`4.09`$ points, from
$`96.92\%`$ to $`101.01\%`$. These quality scores concern model-specific
feasible subsets, however, and do not establish comparable optimization
capability across all instances.

Several models exceed the expert quality reference of $`100\%`$ on their
feasible deliveries, but DAQ places every model below the expert. Grok
4.6 achieves the highest DAQ in the primary comparison at $`86.55\%`$,
leaving a $`13.45`$-point gap. Using
$`\mathrm{DAQ}=\mathrm{Feas}\,Q_{\mathrm{feas}}`$, this gap decomposes
into $`11.61`$ points from infeasible deliveries and $`1.84`$ points
from the net objective shortfall on feasible ones. Thus, approximately
$`86\%`$ of its score deficit comes from the zero credit assigned to
failed deliveries. The dominant observed gap is therefore incomplete
feasible delivery, rather than modest objective shortfalls on successful
cases.

The reliability–quality profile in the right panel of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
reinforces this distinction. Increasing $`\alpha`$ reduces the
compensation that high-scoring instances provide for low-scoring or
infeasible ones. All eleven models retain the same ranking across the 21
plotted values from $`1`$ to $`3`$, while their scores decrease and
remain below the expert reference. The observed ordering is therefore
stable across the tested reliability penalties, but no model closes the
expert gap.

##### Trajectory-based results.

Following
Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Trajectory Analysis Methodology ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"),
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Trajectory-based results. ‣ 4.1 RQ1: Cross-Model Comparison and Performance Against Human Experts ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
summarizes stopping locations along the HCAEU chain (left) and compares
stage quality conditional on a complete chain against model-average DAQ
(right).

Task-equalized complete-chain proportions range from $`24\%`$ for Muse
Spark 1.3 to $`45\%`$ for Grok 4.6, remaining below $`50\%`$ for every
model. The stopping locations reveal distinct gaps in initiating
investigations, testing explanations, and acting on evidence. GPT-5.6
Sol forms no testable hypothesis in $`41\%`$ of opportunities, whereas
Qwen3.8-Max stops at HC and HCAE in $`21\%`$ each. In particular,
stopping at HCAE indicates that evidence has been interpreted without a
linked, evidence-grounded update. Producing an explanation or
interpreting a result is therefore distinct from using that evidence to
revise the working hypothesis or solution. These are gaps in observable
research-chain completion, not proof that every incomplete chain leaves
its issue unsolved.

Conditional stage quality and DAQ also yield different model rankings.
GPT-5.6 Sol combines a DAQ of $`85.02\%`$ with relatively low
conditional stage quality, whereas Qwen3.8-Max has the highest
conditional stage quality but a lower DAQ of $`77.97\%`$. Moreover,
Qwen3.8-Max completes the chain in only $`27\%`$ of research
opportunities. High research quality within completed investigations
does not imply that a model can consistently sustain such investigations
across research opportunities. These findings reveal a key limitation of
current agents: they can occasionally demonstrate strong evidence-based
reasoning, but still lack the reliability to carry investigations from
uncertainty to evidence-grounded revision throughout long-horizon OR
problem solving. Final-delivery performance and sustained research
capability therefore represent distinct dimensions of expertise that
must be evaluated separately.

Figure 4: Research-chain analysis for RQ1. (a) Task-equalized stopping
locations along the HCAEU chain. (b) Mean stage quality among
opportunities with a complete HCAEU chain versus model-average DAQ.

### 4.2 RQ2: Client Information Acquisition Across the OR Workflow

Figure 5: Left: question timing by workflow stage. Segment width shows
the task-equalized question share; height shows the pooled proportion
with confirmed issue resolution. Right: bar length shows the infeasible
rate from
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners");
colored segments show the fixed annotated error-event distribution,
scaled to that length. A trajectory may contain multiple events.

The left panel of
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 RQ2: Client Information Acquisition Across the OR Workflow ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
summarizes the timing and confirmed issue resolution of classifiable
pre-submission client questions. We assign questions to S1–S6 relative
to solver-code development, observed feedback, candidate construction,
self-checking, and final submission. Segment width denotes the
task-equalized question share, and height the pooled
confirmed-resolution proportion. Resolution requires a concrete issue,
targeted action, and confirming outcome; ordinary rule requests and
unresolved or unknown outcomes remain in the denominator when their
stage is known.

Questioning is strongly front-loaded: S1 accounts for
$`86.7\%`$–$`98.3\%`$ of questions across models. Even for Hy4 Preview
and GPT-5.6 Sol, only approximately $`13\%`$ of questions occur after
S1, compared with $`9\%`$ for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Later questions
appear across different stages, including S3–S5, but constitute a small
fraction of total interaction. Despite having access to client
information throughout the workflow, agents predominantly treat
information acquisition as an initial requirement-gathering activity,
rather than consistently revisiting their understanding as solution
development proceeds.

Later-stage interactions nevertheless contribute to confirmed issue
resolution. Confirmed-resolution proportions range from $`10.6\%`$ to
$`37.0\%`$ in S1, compared with approximately $`56\%`$ for
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in S4 and $`71\%`$ for Hy4 Preview in S5. At S4, an
initial candidate already exists; at S5, a complete candidate has been
constructed but has not yet passed self-checking. These observations
show that client clarification can support the diagnosis and correction
of concrete issues after solution construction has begun, rather than
serving only to establish the initial specification.

Taken together, these results reveal a gap between continuous access to
client information and its sustained use during problem solving. Agents
can resolve specific issues through later clarification, yet their
information-seeking behavior remains heavily concentrated before
substantive solver development. A key limitation of current agents is
the lack of a consistent, feedback-responsive process for identifying
and resolving information gaps as solutions evolve. Reliable end-to-end
OR agents should be able to recognize when intermediate results or
execution feedback warrant revisiting business assumptions, seek
targeted clarification, and incorporate the acquired facts into verified
revisions of the formulation or implementation.

### 4.3 RQ3: LLM Failure Patterns in End-to-End OR Projects

Within the annotated trajectories, formulation errors are prominent
across models
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 RQ2: Client Information Acquisition Across the OR Workflow ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"),
right): implementation and delivery (IMP) is the largest error category
for only two of the eleven models. Static constraint errors (CON)
account for $`42.7\%`$ of Claude Opus 5’s error events, while dynamic
and state-transition errors (DYN) account for $`28.7\%`$ and $`25.5\%`$
of those for Hy4 Preview and GLM-5.3-Flash, respectively. Objective and
preference formulation (OBJ) and uncertainty and information structure
(UNC) together account for $`69.0\%`$ of Grok 4.6’s error events and
$`70.5\%`$ of Muse Spark 1.3’s. These profiles identify what requires
correction, rather than providing an additive attribution of each
model’s failure probability.

The distinction is between *solving a specified optimization problem*
and *formulating the right problem from business requirements*. An
executable program may faithfully implement a formulation that
misrepresents the required objectives, state transitions, or information
structure; improving execution alone would not correct that mismatch.
Meanwhile, IMP remains the largest category for GPT-5.6 Sol and Hy3
($`33.3\%`$ and $`33.1\%`$), so implementation failures also persist.
Read alongside RQ1 and RQ2, these findings motivate agents that use both
experimental evidence and client facts to revisit their task
interpretation and revise the adopted solution. The central requirement
is not merely runnable code or plausible numerical outputs, but
consistency from business semantics through formulation, implementation,
and validation.

## 5 Conclusion

OR-License evaluates LLM agents on 31 de-identified OR instances from 10
industrial scenarios using original client materials, ORSim-mediated
interaction, hidden feasibility checks, and client-accepted expert
references. Across eleven evaluated models, several exceed the
expert-normalized objective-quality reference on feasible instances, yet
none matches the expert reference in Deployment-Adjusted Quality.
Trajectory analysis shows that information acquisition continues beyond
initial clarification into solution development and validation; for some
models, later-stage questions are associated with higher confirmed
issue-resolution proportions. These findings motivate better requirement
interpretation, formulation, validation, sustained information-gap
resolution, and evidence-linked self-improvement.

and reformatting, qualitative and thematic data analysis, scientific
figure presentation, manuscript editing, software development, and

All AI-assisted outputs, including reformatted datasets, qualitative and

## Appendix Contents

## Appendix A Metric Definitions and Analysis

This appendix gives the normalization rules, edge-case conventions, and
analytical properties of the metrics introduced in
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

### A.1 Instance-Level Feasibility and Aggregation

Each instance represents one deployment-level delivery and may contain
multiple official test cases. The indicator $`F_{i}`$ in
Equation ([1](#S3.E1 "In Strict Feasibility. ‣ 3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"))
equals one only when the final submission passes the hidden verifier on
every official case. A submission that passes a strict subset of the
cases has $`F_{i}=0`$. This all-cases criterion reflects the delivery
requirement that one solver implementation must satisfy the operational
constraints throughout the instance.

The fixed-denominator metrics $`\mathrm{Feas}`$, DAQ, and
$`\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha}`$ use an instance-level macro-average. Every
instance receives weight $`1/N`$, irrespective of $`|\mathcal{C}_{i}|`$.
Official instances determine the strict feasibility decision and the
within-task objective aggregation, while the cross-instance weight
remains fixed. With $`\mathcal{F}=\{i:F_{i}=1\}`$ and
$`K=|\mathcal{F}|`$, Strict Feasibility is $`\mathrm{Feas}=K/N`$.

### A.2 Objective Normalization and Expert-Relative Quality

For each feasible instance, $`J_{i}^{\mathrm{agent}}`$ and
$`J_{i}^{\mathrm{expert}}`$ denote the instance-level objective values
of the final system submission and the expert reference solution. Both
use the same hidden objective and the same fixed aggregation over
$`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$. Ratio-based comparison requires a strictly positive
scale. When the raw objective is strictly positive, $`T_{i}`$ is the
identity map. Otherwise, the benchmark applies an instance-specific
transformation

|     |                                   |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widetilde{J}_{i}=T_{i}(J_{i})>0,
       ```                                |     |

where $`T_{i}`$ is positive on the evaluated objective domain, applied
identically to every system and the expert reference, and strictly
increasing to preserve the original objective ordering.
Equation ([2](#S3.E2 "In Expert-Relative Quality. ‣ 3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"))
then uses $`\widetilde{J}_{i}`$ for both minimization and maximization
instances.

For Tasks 21 and 22, the economic objective is cumulative return $`R`$,
which is maximized, and the stored evaluation cost is $`C=-R`$. We use
the terminal net asset value factor $`T(R)=1+R=1-C`$, giving
$`Q_{i}=(1-C_{i}^{\mathrm{agent}})/(1-C_{i}^{\mathrm{expert}})`$. All
reported scores for these two tasks use this normalization. Feasibility
follows the verifier outcome independently of objective sign. A passed
run with a missing or nonpositive net asset value factor is explicitly
flagged as a scoring error while retaining its verifier-assigned
feasibility status.

The expert-relative score has a common interpretation across instances:
$`Q_{i}=1`$ matches the expert objective, $`Q_{i}>1`$ improves on it,
and $`Q_{i}<1`$ falls below it. The transformation makes the ratio
dimensionless and anchors every instance at the expert value of one
under the benchmark’s fixed scaling protocol.

The conditional average
$`Q_{\mathrm{feas}}=K^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}Q_{i}`$ measures
solution quality after successful delivery. When $`K=0`$,
$`Q_{\mathrm{feas}}`$ is undefined and reported as N/A. Since
$`\mathcal{F}`$ varies across systems, $`Q_{\mathrm{feas}}`$ serves as a
diagnostic metric. DAQ provides the fixed-denominator overall ranking.

### A.3 DAQ Properties

The gated instance score $`Z_{i}`$ defined in
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
assigns objective quality only to complete deliveries. Therefore an
infeasible instance receives zero deployment-adjusted quality even when
its raw objective value appears favorable. Starting from
Equation ([3](#S3.E3 "In Deployment-Adjusted Quality. ‣ 3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")),
for $`K>0`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{DAQ}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}Q_{i}`$ |  | (5) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{K}{N}\left(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}Q_{i}\right)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\mathrm{Feas}\,Q_{\mathrm{feas}},`$ |  |  |

which establishes the final equality in
Equation ([3](#S3.E3 "In Deployment-Adjusted Quality. ‣ 3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")).
If $`K=0`$, every $`Z_{i}=0`$, so $`\mathrm{DAQ}=0`$ while
$`Q_{\mathrm{feas}}`$ remains N/A. For the expert reference,
$`F_{i}=Q_{i}=Z_{i}=1`$ for every instance, giving
$`\mathrm{DAQ}_{\mathrm{expert}}=1`$.

### A.4 Reliability-Quality Profile

DAQ is the arithmetic mean of the instance scores $`Z_{i}`$, so quality
gains on completed instances can compensate linearly for incomplete
instance coverage. Since $`Q_{i}`$ has no explicit upper cap, a small
number of high-quality solutions can offset failures on other instances.
Equation ([4](#S3.E4 "In Reliability-Quality Profile. ‣ 3.4 Metrics ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"))
exposes this trade-off through a power mean of order $`1/\alpha`$.

At $`\alpha=1`$, the profile recovers the primary metric:

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{DAQ}_{1}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}=\mathrm{DAQ}.
       ```                                                            |     |

For $`\alpha_{2}>\alpha_{1}\geq 1`$, the corresponding power-mean orders
satisfy $`1/\alpha_{2}<1/\alpha_{1}`$. The power-mean inequality
therefore gives

|     |                                                         |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha_{2}}\leq\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha_{1}}.
       ```                                                      |     | (6) |

Increasing $`\alpha`$ raises sensitivity to low instance scores. This
strengthens the penalty on infeasible instances, for which $`Z_{i}=0`$,
and on uneven quality among feasible instances. The expert reference
satisfies $`\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha}=1`$ for every $`\alpha\geq 1`$.

For $`K>0`$, define the conditional power mean

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{\mathrm{feas},\alpha}=\left(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}Q_{i}^{1/\alpha}\right)^{\alpha}.
``` |  |

The profile then decomposes as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\boxed{\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha}=\mathrm{Feas}^{\alpha}Q_{\mathrm{feas},\alpha}}.
``` |  | (7) |

If $`K=0`$, $`\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha}=0`$ for every $`\alpha\geq 1`$.

To illustrate the compensation rate, consider a system that is feasible
on a fraction $`r`$ of the instances and has the same expert-relative
quality $`q`$ on every feasible instance. In this special case,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{DAQ}_{\alpha}=\left(rq^{1/\alpha}\right)^{\alpha}=qr^{\alpha}.
``` |  | (8) |

Matching the expert reference value of one requires $`q=r^{-\alpha}`$.
Larger $`\alpha`$ values therefore require a larger quality gain to
compensate for the same reduction in complete-delivery coverage. For
every finite $`\alpha`$, sufficiently large quality can still compensate
for incomplete coverage; the profile quantifies the required trade-off.

## Appendix B Trajectory Analysis Protocol

This appendix specifies the coding and aggregation rules summarized in
Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Trajectory Analysis Methodology ‣ 3 Benchmark Construction ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

##### Client information acquisition.

Motivated by the information-value view of clarification questions ([Rao
& Daumé III, 2018](#bib.bib39)), we examine when agents ask questions
throughout the solution workflow. We assign each ask action to one of
six event-based stages according to when the question is issued: S1
(before solver code), before the agent first writes substantive code for
solving the task; S2 (before solver feedback), after solver-code
development begins but before the agent observes the first feedback from
a solving attempt; S3 (before the first candidate), after observing this
feedback but before producing the first inspectable candidate containing
concrete business decisions; S4 (before a complete candidate), after the
first candidate appears but before a candidate covers the full required
decision scope; S5 (before passing self-checks), after a complete
candidate is available but before the agent’s own checks report that it
passes; and S6 (before final submission), after passing these
self-checks but before final submission. Self-checks are checks
performed by the agent during the trajectory before final submission. We
also record whether an agent asks again after observing solver feedback,
conditional on having a further decision opportunity.

##### Trajectory error analysis.

Guided by the OR problem-solving workflow ([Hillier et al.,
1995](#bib.bib18)) and prior work on optimization agents
([AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)), we identify confirmed error
events in each agent trajectory and final artifact and classify each
event by its point of origin. We use eight categories: problem
understanding (UND), data and parameter mapping (DATA), decision
representation (DEC), static constraints (CON), dynamic and state
transitions (DYN), uncertainty and information structure (UNC),
objective and preference formulation (OBJ), and implementation and
delivery (IMP). Because a trajectory may contain multiple error events,
category profiles are computed at the event level, with infeasible rates
reported separately. Simulator or infrastructure failures are recorded
separately and are not attributed to the agent.

##### Scientific inquiry.

Drawing on hypothesis–experiment coordination ([Klahr & Dunbar,
1988](#bib.bib23)) and inquiry cycles ([Pedaste et al.,
2015](#bib.bib37)), we analyze research opportunities within agent
trajectories. A research opportunity is a consequential uncertainty
visible to the agent and potentially reducible through investigation,
such as unexpected infeasibility, unexplained objective deterioration,
or an untested modeling assumption. Competing explanations and repeated
experiments addressing the same uncertainty belong to one opportunity.
Domain experts first enumerate research opportunities from each full
recorded trajectory, then annotate stage presence, stage quality, and
chain completion for each opportunity using the fixed inventory.

##### Stage presence and chain completion.

For each opportunity, we independently annotate a testable hypothesis
(H), a mechanistic explanation (C), an executed diagnostic experiment
(A), interpretation of the resulting evidence (E), and an actual
evidence-grounded update (U). Each stage is labeled present, absent, or
indeterminate, with supporting evidence references. A complete HCAEU
chain requires substantively connected evidence within the same issue
and branch: H and C precede A, the observed result of A informs E, and E
leads to a subsequent U. Routine execution or feasibility checking
qualifies as A only when organized as a diagnostic test. U requires an
actual change to the hypothesis, formulation, model, algorithm,
parameters, code, or delivery.

##### Stage-quality rubric.

Each present stage receives a quality score of 1, 2, or 3. For each
stage, we select the highest-quality instance supported by the recorded
evidence within that opportunity. These instances may come from
different branches; chain completion is established separately using
evidence from a single branch. The stage-specific criteria are:

- •
  H: (1) a minimally testable expectation; (2) a specific prediction
  with explicit conditions for support or refutation; (3) predictions
  that distinguish competing explanations.
- •
  C: (1) a directional mechanism linking a factor to an outcome; (2) a
  mechanism with an explicit intervention prediction; (3) an explanation
  that distinguishes competing mechanisms, causal paths, or boundary
  conditions.
- •
  A: (1) a targeted diagnostic test with limited control; (2) an
  explicit baseline or control that largely isolates the key factor; (3)
  an informative experiment that distinguishes competing explanations.
- •
  E: (1) comparison of observations with predictions or candidate
  explanations; (2) identification of explanations supported, refuted,
  or left unresolved; (3) assessment that also accounts for remaining
  uncertainty, alternatives, or evidential limitations.
- •
  U: (1) an actual change linked to preceding evidence; (2) a change
  that directly addresses specific evidence; (3) an evidence-grounded
  revision followed by consistent validation or further targeted
  investigation.

##### Quality aggregation.

We measure stage quality conditional on the opportunity containing a
complete HCAEU chain. Let $`\mathcal{C}_{mt}`$ denote the set of such
opportunities in the selected trajectory for model $`m`$ on task $`t`$,
and let $`q_{is}\in\{1,2,3\}`$ be the quality score for opportunity
$`i`$ and stage $`s\in\mathcal{S}=\{H,C,A,E,U\}`$. The task-level score
is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{mt}=\frac{1}{5|\mathcal{C}_{mt}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{mt}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{q_{is}}{3}.
``` |  | (9) |

Thus, defined scores range from $`1/3`$ to $`1`$.

##### Expert annotation.

OR experts manually annotate all trajectories included in these
analyses, using task specifications, client exchanges, code revisions,
execution feedback, and retained candidate artifacts. Positive
annotations require identifiable supporting evidence.

## Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim

ORSim simulates a business client during an OR engagement. This appendix
describes its design and evaluates its reliability.

### C.1 Simulator Architecture and Selector Variants

##### Design motivation.

To reduce hallucinations in client interactions, we separate evidence
selection from response generation. Prior work has explored several
complementary mechanisms for interactive information elicitation.
[Abdullin et al. (2025)](#bib.bib1) condition a simulated user on the
complete problem statement and introduce comparison-based feedback to
correct the modeling agent’s summaries. AgentMILO ([Gaddam et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14)) uses expert-designed knowledge graphs to guide the
modeling agent’s questions and mathematical formulations. The Human
Imitator ([Duan et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)) is fine-tuned to reproduce
ambiguity and bounded rationality in managerial dialogue, while
$`\tau`$-Rec ([Narasimhan & Narasimhan, 2026](#bib.bib31)) assigns
disclosure tags to private user constraints. Our focus is faithful,
controlled disclosure of instance-specific business knowledge: the
evidence supporting each simulated client reply is explicitly identified
before the reply is generated.

##### Selector–responder architecture.

We first decompose the complete client-side problem statement into a
catalog of business rules, each associated with a stable identifier.
Given an agent’s question, a simulator-side LLM selects relevant rule
identifiers for evidence retrieval. A deterministic controller validates
these identifiers and applies the disclosure policy before passing the
authorized rule texts to the responder. The responder is instructed to
render only the authorized business facts in natural language and to
identify any parts of the question that this evidence leaves unresolved.
The complete rule catalog remains hidden from the evaluated agent. The
selected identifiers make the factual basis of each reply explicit and
inspectable.

##### Ledger schema and disclosure policy.

Each ledger entry has a stable fact_id, one or more source-grounded
answer units, a knowledge_owner label, an in_brief flag, and optional
links to verifier rules or objective components. The owner label
distinguishes client facts from information assigned to the input data,
an external system, or OR expertise. For each query, the deterministic
controller accepts only identifiers that satisfy the ownership and
visibility policy. In the benchmark condition, it allows at most three
newly disclosed non-brief client facts per query; facts already present
in the initial brief may be restated but do not count as newly
disclosed. Requests for input-data, external-system, or OR-expertise
information receive fixed role-specific refusals. The response-only
model receives only the authorized source text, and a failed or unsafe
rendering falls back to that text. Neither the evaluated agent nor the
response model can inspect the complete ledger or hidden evaluator
state.

##### Selector representations.

Related work on evidence-grounded generation has explored fine-grained
propositions ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib9)), hierarchical
summaries ([Sarthi et al., 2024](#bib.bib40)), and knowledge graphs with
community summaries ([Edge et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)). However, advances
in long-context processing also motivate direct access to complete
source information when the knowledge base fits within the available
context budget ([Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Chan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7)). In our setting, this raises the question of whether
an LLM can select relevant rules more reliably from their full texts
than from additional summary or graph representations. Direct access may
preserve conditions and exceptions that intermediate representations
omit, while structured representations may make relevant information
easier to locate. We therefore investigate three selector designs:

(1) Flat selector. The selector receives the question together with the
complete catalog of rule identifiers and full rule texts. It directly
selects the identifiers needed to answer the question, without an
intermediate summary index or knowledge graph. All candidate rules are
available for joint consideration in a single selection step, including
details whose relevance becomes apparent only in relation to other
rules.

(2) Summary-plus-detail selector. Concise summaries provide an index for
locating relevant rules, while the corresponding full rule texts provide
the evidence for response generation. The selector uses the summaries to
identify relevant content and retrieves the associated details. This
reduces the amount of text used for initial selection, but may overlook
rules whose relevance depends on conditions or exceptions omitted from
their summaries.

(3) Summary-plus-KG selector. A textual overview provides global
context, while a knowledge graph organizes business entities and their
relations. The selector uses both representations to identify relevant
knowledge and select the associated business-rule texts as answer
evidence. This design makes relational structure explicit, but
introduces additional opportunities for information loss or distortion
during graph construction and graph-based selection.

We ultimately adopt the flat selector as the default implementation. It
keeps the complete rule details available during selection while
avoiding intermediate summary-based filtering or graph construction.
Crucially, access to the full catalog is limited to the selection stage:
the responder still receives only selected, authorized evidence. We
evaluate the resulting simulator’s reliability below.

### C.2 Reliability Analysis

We evaluate the simulator at two levels: whether the selector identifies
the business rules needed to answer a question, and whether the
resulting reply faithfully satisfies the reference requirements while
respecting the client’s information boundary. We also examine
consistency across repeated runs, since occasional unsupported or
incomplete replies can introduce noise into the evaluation of the
optimization agent.

Response-level metrics are derived from a shared set of component
annotations, whose inter-annotator agreement is assessed separately.

##### Evaluation setup.

We construct an expert-annotated evaluation set containing 204 queries
across 5 benchmark instances. The set includes 119 standard queries and
85 adversarial queries. Standard queries cover individual business
rules, questions requiring multiple rules, and conditions or exceptions
that must be preserved in the answer. Adversarial queries probe
unsupported assumptions, requests to invent missing information, and
attempts to obtain information or OR advice outside the simulated
client’s role.

For each query, domain experts annotate the relevant, disclosable
business-rule identifiers and the expected response requirements. These
specify both the information that should be conveyed and any required
correction, acknowledgment of insufficient information, or refusal.
Questions that depend on earlier exchanges are paired with a fixed
dialogue history and disclosure state. The reference annotations are
shared across selector variants but are not available to the simulator.

##### Compared variants.

We compare the flat, summary-plus-detail, and summary-plus-KG selectors
described in
Section [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Simulator Architecture and Selector Variants ‣ Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

All three selector variants use the same underlying business-rule
catalog, disclosure policy, and responder. We hold the selector
backbone, responder backbone, and decoding settings fixed, so that the
comparison isolates the effect of the selector representation and
selection procedure.

The simulator uses DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

Each query is evaluated in 5 independent runs per selector variant, with
its initial dialogue history and disclosure state restored before every
run. This produces $`204\times 3\times 5=3{,}060`$ replies. Each
selector variant therefore contributes $`119\times 5=595`$ replies to
standard queries and $`85\times 5=425`$ replies to adversarial queries.

##### Full-statement direct-answer baseline.

We additionally include an end-to-end baseline in which the responder
uses the complete problem statement as evidence to answer the query
directly. We match the responder backbone, decoding settings, fixed
dialogue context, and disclosure policy across configurations. This
comparison characterizes the end-to-end configurations, jointly varying
source representation and evidence provision.

The full-statement results cover $`204\times 5=1{,}020`$ replies, with
the same split of 119 standard and 85 adversarial queries and five runs
per query. The 3,060 replies, 6,120 reply-review assignments, and
annotation agreement statistics reported for the three-selector
evaluation remain restricted to the three selector variants.

##### Rule-selection accuracy.

Let $`G_{q}`$ denote the reference rule set for query $`q`$, and let
$`S_{q,j}`$ denote the identifiers returned by the selector in run
$`j`$, with the variant index omitted for readability. For queries with
$`G_{q}\neq\varnothing`$, we compute

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Precision}_{q,j}=\frac{|S_{q,j}\cap G_{q}|}{\max(1,|S_{q,j}|)},\qquad\mathrm{Recall}_{q,j}=\frac{|S_{q,j}\cap G_{q}|}{|G_{q}|}.
``` |  | (10) |

Precision measures whether the selected rules belong to the relevant,
disclosable reference set; recall measures whether the selector recovers
the reference evidence, including necessary conditions and exceptions.
For a given query category, let $`\mathcal{Q}^{+}`$ be the subset of
queries with nonempty reference rule sets. We average over runs and then
over eligible queries:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{P}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}}\sum_{j=1}^{5}\mathrm{Precision}_{q,j}}{5|\mathcal{Q}^{+}|},`$ |  | (11) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{R}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}}\sum_{j=1}^{5}\mathrm{Recall}_{q,j}}{5|\mathcal{Q}^{+}|}.`$ |  |  |

P and R are computed automatically from the selected and reference rule
identifiers, then averaged over runs and queries with nonempty reference
rule sets. Queries with no disclosable reference rules are assessed
using reply-level criteria for the expected response behavior.

##### Reply-level rule coverage for the direct-answer baseline.

Selector-level P and R are not applicable to full-statement direct
answering because no selector returns rule identifiers. We therefore
report them as “—” for this baseline and keep the following reply-level
diagnostic separate. Let $`O_{q,j}`$ denote the distinct catalog rules
actually conveyed by the reply, determined by mapping its content to
rule identifiers after generation. For $`G_{q}\neq\varnothing`$, define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P^{\mathrm{out}}_{q,j}=\frac{|O_{q,j}\cap G_{q}|}{\max(1,|O_{q,j}|)},\qquad R^{\mathrm{out}}_{q,j}=\frac{|O_{q,j}\cap G_{q}|}{|G_{q}|}.
``` |  | (12) |

As with rule-selection accuracy, we average over the five runs and then
over queries with nonempty reference rule sets. The baseline uses 119
eligible standard queries and 54 eligible adversarial queries. These
output-level scores are not directly comparable to selector-level P/R:
comparing variants on this diagnostic requires the same reply-to-rule
mapping for every variant. Unmapped factual claims remain subject to
claim-level support evaluation.

##### Response faithfulness and disclosure compliance.

We evaluate generated replies separately from the selected rule
identifiers. Following claim-level assessments of faithfulness ([Es
et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)), we decompose each reply $`r`$ into a fixed
set of atomic factual claims $`\mathcal{C}_{r}`$ before independent
support annotation. Both reviewers receive the same claim decomposition.
The decomposition preserves each claim’s quantities, conditions, and
exceptions.

For each claim $`c\in\mathcal{C}_{r}`$, the binary label $`h_{r,c}`$
equals 1 if the claim is supported by authorized evidence actually
provided to the responder, and 0 otherwise. For the three selector
variants, this is the selected, authorized evidence. The same
authorization standard applies to the full-statement baseline: a fact
appearing in the complete statement is not automatically authorized for
disclosure.

For each reply, the binary label $`d_{r}`$ equals 1 if the reply
respects the disclosure policy and the client’s assigned role, and 0 if
it reveals prohibited information or provides out-of-role advice.

For the set of replies $`\mathcal{R}`$ associated with a particular
variant and query category, we compute

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Faith.}=\frac{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{r}}h_{r,c}}{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}|\mathcal{C}_{r}|},\qquad\mathrm{Viol.}=\frac{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}(1-d_{r})}{|\mathcal{R}|}.
``` |  | (13) |

Faithfulness therefore pools factual claims across replies, whereas the
disclosure violation rate counts replies. Replies without factual claims
do not contribute to the faithfulness denominator, but remain eligible
for disclosure and end-to-end evaluation. If an entire evaluation group
contains no factual claims, its faithfulness score is reported as not
applicable.

##### End-to-end reply reliability.

We additionally annotate a binary reference-fulfillment label $`t_{r}`$.
This label equals 1 only when the reply conveys all required,
disclosable information and satisfies the expected response behavior
specified by the reference annotation. It jointly captures information
completeness and any required correction, acknowledgment of insufficient
information, or refusal. For partially answerable questions, both the
answerable content and the required handling of the unresolved part must
be correct.

The binary success label is derived deterministically:

|     |                                                       |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       y_{r}=t_{r}\,d_{r}\prod_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{r}}h_{r,c}.
       ```                                                    |     | (14) |

Thus, success requires reference fulfillment, disclosure compliance, and
support for every factual claim. For replies without factual claims, the
empty product is defined as 1; success still requires $`t_{r}=d_{r}=1`$.
Refusing an answerable question therefore does not count as success,
even if the reply contains no unsupported factual claims. No additional
holistic success judgment is collected.

To measure consistency, we adapt the $`\mathrm{pass}^{k}`$ metric of
$`\tau`$-bench ([Yao et al., 2024](#bib.bib50)). For $`Q`$ queries
evaluated with $`n`$ independent runs each, let
$`c_{q}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}y_{q,j}`$ be the number of successful replies to
query $`q`$. We estimate

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{pass}^{k}=\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\frac{\binom{c_{q}}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},\qquad n\geq k,
``` |  | (15) |

where $`\binom{c_{q}}{k}=0`$ when $`c_{q}<k`$.

With $`n=5`$, the reported metrics simplify to

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{pass}^{1}=\frac{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}c_{q}}{5Q},\qquad\mathrm{pass}^{5}=\frac{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\mathbf{1}[c_{q}=5]}{Q}.
``` |  | (16) |

The former counts successful replies; the latter counts queries for
which all five replies are successful. Accordingly, the denominators are
595 and 119 for standard queries, and 425 and 85 for adversarial
queries, respectively, for each variant.

These metrics assess simulator reply reliability.

##### Human annotation and agreement.

Ten domain experts annotate the 3,060 replies generated by the three
selector variants. Each reply is independently reviewed by two experts,
yielding 6,120 reply-review assignments. The full-statement baseline is
excluded from this agreement analysis.

Reviewers receive the query, fixed dialogue context, reference
requirements, disclosure policy, and authorized evidence provided to the
responder. They are blinded to the selector variant and each other’s
judgments. Using a shared rubric, each reviewer labels claim-level
evidence support ($`h`$), reply-level reference fulfillment ($`t`$), and
disclosure compliance ($`d`$). A reviewer-specific success label ($`y`$)
is then derived from these annotations using
Equation [14](#A3.E14 "In End-to-end reply reliability. ‣ C.2 Reliability Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

We measure pre-adjudication agreement for all three components and the
derived success label. Because reviewer pairs vary across replies, we
use nominal Krippendorff’s $`\alpha`$ ([Krippendorff,
2011](#bib.bib24)), treating unassigned reviewer–unit entries as
missing.

For annotation dimension $`\ell`$, let $`U_{\ell}`$ denote the number of
double-annotated units and $`A_{\ell}`$ the number on which both
reviewers agree. Let $`m_{\ell,0}`$ and $`m_{\ell,1}`$ denote the pooled
counts of binary labels, with $`m_{\ell,0}+m_{\ell,1}=2U_{\ell}`$. We
compute

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Agreement}_{\ell}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{A_{\ell}}{U_{\ell}},`$ | $`\displaystyle D_{o,\ell}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{U_{\ell}-A_{\ell}}{U_{\ell}},`$ |  | (17) |
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{e,\ell}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{2m_{\ell,0}m_{\ell,1}}{(2U_{\ell})(2U_{\ell}-1)},`$ | $`\displaystyle\alpha_{\ell}`$ | $`\displaystyle=1-\frac{D_{o,\ell}}{D_{e,\ell}}.`$ |  |  |

Evidence support is evaluated over $`U_{h}=5{,}293`$ factual claims; the
remaining dimensions each cover $`U_{t}=U_{d}=U_{y}=3{,}060`$ replies.
When $`D_{e,\ell}=0`$, we report $`\alpha_{\ell}`$ as not applicable and
provide the raw agreement and label counts.

Table [2](#A3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Human annotation and agreement. ‣ C.2 Reliability Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
summarizes the results. Raw agreement ranges from 97.58% to 99.31%, and
Krippendorff’s $`\alpha`$ ranges from 0.831 to 0.920 across the four
dimensions.

Disagreements are adjudicated using the source rules, reference
requirements, and disclosure policy. Final response metrics use one
adjudicated label per claim or reply, with success recomputed from the
adjudicated components using
Equation [14](#A3.E14 "In End-to-end reply reliability. ‣ C.2 Reliability Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

|                       |       |                 |                             |
|-----------------------|-------|-----------------|-----------------------------|
| Annotation            | Unit  |  Raw agreement  |  Krippendorff’s $`\alpha`$  |
| Evidence support      | Claim | $`98.53\%`$     | $`0.920`$                   |
| Reference fulfillment | Reply | $`98.10\%`$     | $`0.831`$                   |
| Disclosure compliance | Reply | $`99.31\%`$     | $`0.866`$                   |
| Derived reply success | Reply | $`97.58\%`$     | $`0.873`$                   |

and rounded to three decimal places.

##### Results.

The flat selector achieves the best observed value on all six metrics
among the three selector variants, for both standard and adversarial
queries
(Table [3](#A3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Results. ‣ C.2 Reliability Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")).
Its rule-selection precision and recall are 95.64% and 98.01% on
standard queries, and 97.22% and 99.26% on eligible adversarial queries.
Its advantage is larger on the adversarial subset: precision exceeds
summary-plus-detail and summary-plus-KG by 13.48 and 10.97 percentage
points, respectively, while recall improves by 12.69 and 10.51 points.
Thus, the additional summary or KG structure does not improve
rule-selection accuracy in this evaluation.

The response-level results also favor the flat selector. On standard
queries, its faithfulness is 98.71%, compared with 87.50% for
summary-plus-detail and 74.50% for summary-plus-KG. On adversarial
queries, the corresponding values are 96.55%, 94.98%, and 90.17%. The
flat selector produces only two disclosure violations among 595 standard
replies (0.34%) and one among 425 adversarial replies (0.24%). The
corresponding violation rates are 3.19% and 4.00% for
summary-plus-detail, and 2.86% and 3.29% for summary-plus-KG. High
claim-level faithfulness alone does not ensure end-to-end success:
summary-plus-detail achieves 94.98% faithfulness on adversarial queries
but only 76.24% $`\mathrm{pass}^{1}`$. The latter is a reply-level
criterion requiring support for every factual claim, complete reference
fulfillment, and disclosure compliance.

For end-to-end reliability, the flat selector achieves
$`\mathrm{pass}^{1}`$ of 95.46% on standard queries and 98.82% on
adversarial queries. These values exceed summary-plus-detail by 6.22 and
22.59 percentage points, and summary-plus-KG by 7.56 and 17.18 points,
respectively. Its $`\mathrm{pass}^{5}`$ is 94.12% in both categories,
corresponding to 112 of 119 standard queries and 80 of 85 adversarial
queries. Relative to the two structured selectors, the
$`\mathrm{pass}^{5}`$ advantage ranges from 12.61 to 14.29 points on
standard queries and from 24.71 to 31.76 points on adversarial queries.

The structured selectors also illustrate why average success and
repeated-run consistency should be reported separately.

On adversarial queries, summary-plus-KG has higher $`\mathrm{pass}^{1}`$
than summary-plus-detail (81.65% versus 76.24%), but lower
$`\mathrm{pass}^{5}`$ (62.35% versus 69.41%).

Although summary-plus-KG produces fewer failed replies (78 versus 101),
those failures affect more queries (32 versus 26). A higher average
reply success rate therefore does not necessarily mean that more queries
are answered successfully in every run.

These results support using the flat selector in ORSim. Across both
query categories, 32 of its 1,020 replies fail the success criterion,
and 12 of its 204 queries have at least one failed run.

Table [4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Full-statement baseline results. ‣ C.2 Reliability Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").
Faith. is the percentage of supported factual claims. Viol. and
$`\mathrm{pass}^{1}`$ are the percentages of violating and successful
replies, respectively; $`\mathrm{pass}^{5}`$ is the percentage of
queries with five successful replies. Annotation agreement in
Table [2](#A3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Human annotation and agreement. ‣ C.2 Reliability Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
covers the three selector variants. Percentages and percentage-point
differences are calculated before rounding and reported to two decimal
places.

##### Full-statement baseline results.

The full-statement baseline exhibits low reply-level precision, high
reply-level recall, and substantial disclosure violations. As shown in
Table [4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Full-statement baseline results. ‣ C.2 Reliability Analysis ‣ Appendix C Details and Reliability of ORSim ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"),
reply-level precision is 50.41% on standard queries and 39.30% on
adversarial queries, while recall is 95.94% and 94.31%, respectively.
The baseline therefore combines broad coverage of required rules with
the output of many additional rules. Its 3,979 standard-query claims and
2,590 adversarial-query claims correspond to 6.69 and 6.09 claims per
reply.

Extra information, unsupported information, and prohibited disclosure
remain distinct. Additional information that is authorized and supported
can reduce reply-level precision without necessarily reducing
faithfulness or violating the disclosure policy. Conversely, access to a
complete statement does not make every fact disclosable, nor does it
authorize out-of-role advice. For this baseline, faithfulness is 94.47%
on standard queries and 87.03% on adversarial queries, while 168 of 595
standard replies (28.24%) and 201 of 425 adversarial replies (47.29%)
violate the disclosure policy. These results show that high claim-level
support and substantial reply-level violations coexist in this
configuration.

Finally, high reply-level recall alone does not guarantee end-to-end
success. The baseline has 384 of 595 successful standard replies
($`\mathrm{pass}^{1}=64.54\%`$), but only 49 of 119 standard queries
succeed in every run ($`\mathrm{pass}^{5}=41.18\%`$). For adversarial
queries, the corresponding counts are 176 of 425 replies (41.41%) and 16
of 85 queries (18.82%). These values follow the same success definition,
which jointly requires reference fulfillment, disclosure compliance, and
support for every factual claim.

## Appendix D Implementation Details

### D.1 Agent Harness Selection

Our benchmark evaluates the complete OR workflow. A system must inspect
briefs and input files, create and edit solver code, execute that code,
inspect solver outputs, and revise the delivery after feedback.
Coding-agent harnesses expose these shell-based and file-based
interaction primitives and have become a common substrate for
long-horizon model evaluation and training ([Cao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6); [Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib19); [Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib48); [OpenAI, 2026b](#bib.bib34); [Opsahl-Ong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib35); [Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib25)).

We therefore use Claude Code as the primary harness. This choice fixes a
common interaction surface across evaluated models and reduces variation
caused by adaptation to a benchmark-specific tool-calling API. Agents
access ORSim through the Bash command ask, while file inspection,
editing, solver execution, and feedback remain available through the
harness. The harness supplies execution mechanics only; it does not
provide OR modeling expertise or access to hidden evaluator state. Model
versions, budgets, and decoding settings are reported in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Settings ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"),
and interface sensitivity is examined with the Codex ablation in
Appendix [D.7](#A4.SS7 "D.7 Harness Ablation ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

### D.2 Models

We evaluate the eleven models listed in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"):
Claude Opus 5 ([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib4)),
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ([DeepSeek, 2026](#bib.bib10)), Gemini 3.8
Flash ([Google, 2026](#bib.bib15)), GLM-5.3-Flash ([Z.AI,
2026](#bib.bib51)), Grok 4.6 ([xAI, 2026](#bib.bib47)), GPT-5.6
Sol ([OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib33)), Hy3 ([Tencent, 2026a](#bib.bib43)),
Hy4 preview ([Tencent, 2026b](#bib.bib44)), Muse Spark 1.3 ([Meta,
2026](#bib.bib30)), Qwen3.8-Max ([Alibaba Group, 2026](#bib.bib3)), and
Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro ([ByteDance Seed Team, 2026](#bib.bib5)).

### D.3 Settings

We use Harbor 0.18.0 as the execution framework. The harness versions
used in our experiments are Claude Code 2.1.278 and Codex 0.155.1. The
interaction policy imposes a hard maximum of 500 rounds. Harbor-native
tasks are allocated a 12-hour (43,200-s) wall-clock budget, and each
solver invocation is limited to 3,600 s, including the solver subprocess
and feedback paths. These values are upper bounds; an episode may
terminate earlier after successful completion or verification.

Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.3 Settings ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")

listed in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").
“Max context” denotes the effective context cap enforced by the gateway,
and “thinking strength” denotes the request-level reasoning control.

### D.4 Semantic Validation

Bike-sharing Tasks 26–31 require additional semantic validation due to
their specialized modeling requirements involving scenario structures,
risk preferences, and rolling optimization. These requirements concern
not only the feasibility and objective quality of final decisions, but
also whether the underlying solver correctly implements the prescribed
optimization formulations and decision processes, which cannot be fully
verified through deterministic checks alone.

For these tasks, all results reported in this paper were manually
reviewed by human experts. To facilitate community use, we also provide
a human-validated LLM-as-a-judge protocol for this semantic review. The
recorded judge configuration specifies DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a maximum
output length of 393,216 tokens, and high reasoning strength. To
validate this protocol, each task was judged five times, and every
judgment was independently checked by two human experts. All judgments
agreed with both human assessments, supporting the reliability of this
configuration within our evaluation setting. The prompts are presented
in
Appendix [D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Prompts ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").
````
