## Appendix E Solution Strategies and Optimization-Structure Exploitation

To characterize how LLMs select and organize optimization methods, we
annotate the final adopted solution strategy along three dimensions:
solution techniques (T), objective handling (O), and problem-structure
exploitation (S). Annotations concern the final submitted program and
the computational workflow that produces the submitted solution.
Abandoned approaches and unused code are excluded, and default
mechanisms internal to a solver are not attributed as additional
agent-designed methods. The three dimensions characterize algorithm and
tool use, objective design, and the recognition and exploitation of
optimization structure, respectively.

### E.1 Annotation Framework

##### Solution techniques (T).

This dimension identifies the algorithmic mechanisms used to generate
decisions. We distinguish seven categories: general-purpose optimization
solver invocation (T1), specialized structural algorithms or analytical
methods (T2), greedy or rule-based construction (T3), local or
neighborhood search (T4), metaheuristics or randomized optimization
(T5), enumeration (T6), and branching search (T7). T6 covers explicit
generation and evaluation or filtering of a finite collection of
candidates. T7 covers an explicitly controlled tree of partial decisions
in which branches are expanded and excluded. Branch-and-bound, pruning,
and heuristics performed internally by a general-purpose solver are
subsumed under T1. A hybrid strategy may receive multiple labels when
distinct modules participate in the adopted workflow. Operations within
a single complete algorithm are not counted repeatedly; for example,
neighborhood moves internal to a metaheuristic do not independently
receive T4.

##### Objective handling (O).

This dimension identifies the criterion guiding decisions at the level
of the overall task. We assign one of two mutually exclusive labels:
direct business-objective handling (O1) or autonomous
surrogate-objective handling (O2). O1 covers direct optimization of the
prescribed business objectives and equivalent treatments that preserve
their priority relationships, including optimization of a prescribed
secondary objective within the primary-optimal solution set. O2 covers
independently designed scores, weights, or local subobjectives that
substitute for the complete business objective to guide construction or
staged optimization. The absence of an explicit mathematical objective
in the problem statement does not by itself imply O2: faithfully
translating a business requirement into a mathematical expression
remains O1. The labels depend on the criterion governing solution
selection and are independent of whether the agent or expert wrote the
objective expression.

##### Problem-structure exploitation (S).

This dimension identifies structural properties actively exploited to
organize, simplify, or restrict optimization. We distinguish four
categories: equivalent compression and reformulation (S1), autonomous
decomposition (S2), specialized structural algorithm exploitation (S3),
and valid tightening or search-space reduction (S4). S1 includes
justified aggregation, variable elimination, and compact equivalent
representations of models or objectives. S2 includes autonomously chosen
rolling schemes, task or resource decomposition, and state propagation
or coordination between subproblems. S3 requires identifying an
applicable matching, network-flow, dynamic-programming, or other
specialized structure and actually using the corresponding algorithm. S4
covers valid bounds, dominance relations, symmetry reduction, or
objective-value restrictions used to narrow subsequent search. Merely
implementing explicitly required multiple periods, scenarios, or
decision rounds does not qualify as additional structural exploitation.
Multiple distinct structural operations may receive multiple labels.

##### Relationships between the dimensions.

The three dimensions describe different aspects of a strategy and can
jointly characterize the same workflow. For example, an autonomously
designed rolling scheduling strategy receives S2 when it divides the
planning task into successive subproblems and propagates state between
them. Within each window, decisions may be generated by an optimization
solver or by rule-based construction, corresponding to T1 or T3. The
window-level criterion may preserve the prescribed business objective or
replace it with an independently designed guidance score, corresponding
to O1 or O2. Rolling execution alone therefore determines neither the
technique label nor the objective-handling label.

As a second example, consider a strategy that first establishes the
primary optimum, then adds a constraint preserving that value and solves
a second model for the prescribed secondary objective. This strategy can
receive T1, O1, and S4: T1 records solver invocation, O1 records
preservation of the prescribed objective hierarchy, and S4 records the
use of the primary optimum to restrict subsequent optimization. The
labels describe strategies and their combinations; adoption frequency
itself is not a score of method quality.

### E.2 Strategy Patterns and Expert Comparison

Figures [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ E.2 Strategy Patterns and Expert Comparison ‣ Appendix E Solution Strategies and Optimization-Structure Exploitation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
and [7](#A5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ E.2 Strategy Patterns and Expert Comparison ‣ Appendix E Solution Strategies and Optimization-Structure Exploitation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
summarize adoption rates across models and the expert reference
solutions. Aggregate agent rates weight tasks equally within each model
and then average equally across models. The results show that LLMs can
combine optimization tools, candidate construction, and search
procedures, while their differences from the expert extend to how these
mechanisms connect objectives with problem structure.

##### From tool invocation to method composition.

As shown in
Figure [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ E.2 Strategy Patterns and Expert Comparison ‣ Appendix E Solution Strategies and Optimization-Structure Exploitation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners"),
agents invoke general-purpose optimization solvers (T1) in 78.0% of
tasks, compared with 93.5% for the expert. Conversely, greedy or
rule-based construction (T3) is more frequent among agents (29.6%) than
in the expert solutions (19.4%). General-purpose solvers are therefore a
central component of LLM-generated solutions, alongside procedures that
construct decisions through successive selection, assignment, or
ordering. These techniques can contribute jointly to the final solution:
an agent may construct candidates before selecting among them with a
solver, or adjust an initial solver-generated solution. Tool-use
capability thus includes composing methods into an executable solution
process, beyond invoking an optimization library.

##### Instance-specific methods and paths to scalability.

Explicit enumeration (T6) appears in 12.3% of agent solutions, compared
with 3.2% of expert solutions. In the trajectories, enumeration is
mainly used to generate local feasible combinations, construct batch or
wave catalogs, and compare finite parameter configurations, followed by
selection through a solver or an evaluation rule. These approaches
demonstrate the ability to devise direct methods for the current
instance: when the candidate space is manageable, explicit generation
and comparison provide a clear and readily implementable solution
procedure.

The computational demands of such procedures depend strongly on the size
of the candidate space. Combinatorial enumeration can grow
exponentially, and even enumeration of fixed-size combinations can
produce rapidly expanding candidate catalogs. Some expert solutions
instead use rule-based construction, neighborhood improvement, or
coordinated decomposition to generate and improve solutions
progressively, with adjustable iteration budgets, neighborhood sizes, or
search effort. The contrast reveals different design tendencies: agents
more frequently handle candidates explicitly for the current instance,
whereas expert solutions more often retain iterative mechanisms that
offer paths for accommodating larger problems.

##### Reformulating representations and organizing structured search.

Figure [7](#A5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ E.2 Strategy Patterns and Expert Comparison ‣ Appendix E Solution Strategies and Optimization-Structure Exploitation ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
shows that equivalent compression and reformulation (S1) are more
frequent among agents (13.2%) than in the expert solutions (6.5%).
Autonomous decomposition (S2) and valid tightening or search-space
reduction (S4), by contrast, are less frequent among agents: 23.2% and
27.3%, respectively, compared with 41.9% and 45.2% for the expert.
Agents often use aggregation, precomputation, and compact
representations to transform a problem into a form suitable for
subsequent optimization. The expert more frequently organizes the
solution process through rolling windows, subproblem partitioning, state
propagation, and valid bounds.

Both exploit problem structure, but at different points in the solution
process: agent strategies more often emphasize representation changes,
while expert strategies more often use structure throughout the
organization of search. Agent use of S1 is also concentrated across
tasks: Tasks 12 and 30 account for 44.4% of all positive S1 annotations.
This concentration indicates consistent treatment of particular
structures rather than a uniform tendency across problem types.

##### Tool use and objective design are distinct capabilities.

Agents use autonomous surrogate objectives (O2) in 26.4% of tasks,
compared with 38.7% for the expert. Among the expert’s O2 solutions,
83.3% also invoke a general-purpose solver. Meanwhile, 49.5% of agent
solutions using greedy or rule-based construction retain the direct
business objective (O1). Solution techniques and objective handling
therefore do not have a one-to-one correspondence. The expert may
optimize a self-designed local score or surrogate objective with a
solver to guide complex decisions. Agents may also generate candidates
through rules and then select among them using the full business
objective.

These combinations distinguish the ability to use optimization tools
from the ability to design optimization guidance and preserve the
business evaluation criterion. The higher agent adoption of O1 reflects
a greater tendency to retain direct business evaluation, whereas the
higher expert adoption of O2 reflects more frequent use of autonomous
objective design to organize local or staged optimization.

##### Different models emphasize different capabilities.

Across models, general-purpose solver adoption ranges from 67.7% to
87.1%, surrogate-objective adoption from 16.1% to 48.4%, and tightening
or search-space reduction from 9.7% to 41.9%. The model whose adoption
rate is closest to the expert also varies by dimension.
Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro and Qwen3.8-Max both invoke solvers in 87.1% of
tasks, closest to the expert’s 93.5%. Gemini 3.8 Flash uses surrogate
objectives in 35.5% of tasks, close to the expert’s 38.7%. Grok 4.6 has
the closest autonomous-decomposition rate (35.5%, compared with 41.9%),
while GLM-5.3-Flash has the closest tightening and search-reduction rate
(41.9%, compared with 45.2%).

These profiles show that frequent solver use does not necessarily
coincide with frequent autonomous objective design or structured search.
The joint T–O–S analysis exposes differences that a single
tool-invocation rate cannot capture: LLMs demonstrate capabilities in
devising instance-specific methods and reformulating problem
representations, while connecting objective design, subproblem
organization, and search control into a complete solution process
remains a deeper distinction from the expert reference solutions.

before benchmark construction (✓: yes; ✗: no).

##### Optimization modeling and constraint reasoning.

A major line of work evaluates the ability to translate prepared problem
descriptions into optimization models or solve explicitly specified
optimization tasks. NL4Opt uses annotated linear-programming word
problems ([Ramamonjison et al., 2023](#bib.bib38)), while Mamo draws on
academic materials ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)) and OptiBench
collects problems from textbooks, assignments, and examinations ([Yang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib49)). IndustryOR brings industrial content into
this setting through abstracted industrial optimization problems ([Huang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)). Complementing these sources, OptMATH-Bench
uses bidirectional data synthesis ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)), and
ConstraintBench constructs synthetic OR scenarios for evaluating
constraint reasoning ([Tso et al., 2026](#bib.bib45)). These benchmarks
support systematic evaluation of modeling and reasoning under a prepared
task specification, centering on the accurate encoding of supplied
requirements. OR-License starts from original business requirements and
input formats preserved through de-identification, with partial
requirements disclosed in the initial brief. Agents establish the
relevant specification by acquiring additional client-held facts and
integrating them into the development of an executable solution. This
setting evaluates requirement acquisition, interpretation, and
formalization together with solver development.

##### Combinatorial optimization and algorithm engineering.

Another line of evaluation emphasizes computational problem solving and
the development of effective algorithms. GraphArena evaluates graph
computation using public graph datasets ([Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib42)). Agent-oriented benchmarks extend evaluation to
algorithm search and implementation: CO-Bench draws on OR-Library and
the optimization literature ([Sun et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)); RoutBench,
introduced with ARS, uses synthetic vehicle-routing variants ([Li
et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)); HeuriGym draws on open-source projects and
research papers to evaluate LLM-crafted heuristics ([Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib8)); and ALE-Bench uses AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems
for long-horizon, objective-driven algorithm engineering ([Imajuku
et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)). These agent-oriented benchmarks evaluate
multi-step work and executable outcomes for specified optimization
tasks. Their central challenge is selecting, implementing, and refining
methods that produce competitive solutions from supplied task
definitions. OR-License combines this algorithmic work with the
acquisition and interpretation of client requirements. The resulting
evaluation covers both establishing the optimization task and developing
a solution that satisfies its operational constraints and achieves
competitive objective quality.

##### Multi-stage OR agent benchmarks.

OR-Space and ORAgentBench are particularly close to our setting because
they broaden OR evaluation to executable environments and multi-stage
agent workflows. OR-Space reconstructs IndustryOR problems as multi-file
workspaces ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib52)). ORAgentBench draws on OR
papers, benchmark seeds, and operational scenarios, and includes
scripted event updates ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib25)). These
environments evaluate agents that inspect task assets, implement
solutions, and complete several stages of optimization. OR-License uses
original client materials as the starting point for this workflow.
Agents can elicit missing business facts as information needs arise
during formulation, solving, and refinement, and their final deliveries
are compared with client-accepted expert references from the original
engagements. This connects multi-stage agent evaluation to the
requirements, information boundaries, and completed deliveries of the
source projects.

##### Professional-work and long-horizon agent benchmarks.

Beyond OR, recent benchmarks make completed professional work products
and sustained execution central units of evaluation. GDPval uses
professional work products adapted by experts ([Patwardhan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36)), APEX-Agents provides expert-constructed professional
workspaces ([Vidgen et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)), and AgencyBench curates
tasks from real-world AI usage and includes rubric-based feedback ([Li
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib27)). Their emphasis on completed deliverables
and sustained execution provides a broader context for evaluating
economically relevant work. OR-License specializes this direction to OR
deliveries, where an executable decision must satisfy operational
constraints before its objective quality can be meaningfully assessed.
Our construction links each evaluated delivery to the original client
requirements, the information available during the engagement, and the
expert solution ultimately accepted by the client.

##### Client interaction as information acquisition.

The client-interaction column characterizes how agents receive
task-relevant information during an episode. File inspection gives
access to supplied materials, and solver feedback reports computational
outcomes under the agent’s current formulation. ORAgentBench supplies
scripted event updates ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib25)), while
AgencyBench supports deliverable revision through rubric-based
feedback ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib27)). Interactive user simulation
appears in customer-service settings such as $`\tau`$-bench ([Yao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib50)), and elicitation has been studied in
optimization modeling dialogues ([Abdullin et al., 2025](#bib.bib1));
OR-License differs by tying elicited business facts to executable
optimization deliverables. Client fact elicitation evaluates how agents
identify missing business requirements, formulate questions, and
incorporate the resulting answers into their solutions. GDPval
explicitly acknowledges that supplying the full task context leaves out
the work required to establish that context ([Patwardhan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36)). In OR-License, agents receive an initial business
brief and the task input files, while additional client-held facts are
accessible through ORSim. Client interaction remains available
throughout formulation, solving, and refinement, allowing agents to
revisit requirements as new information needs arise. The simulated
client provides authorized business facts; the agent is responsible for
mathematical formulations and algorithmic choices. This design makes
identifying information gaps, asking relevant questions, and
incorporating the answers part of the same optimization episode, with
explicit responsibilities for the client and the OR agent.

##### Original materials and client-accepted reference solutions.

The comparison tracks the provenance of both task inputs and reference
solutions. The *original client materials* criterion requires original
project requirements and inputs preserved through de-identification
only. The *client-accepted references* criterion requires that reference
solutions were accepted in the original professional engagements before
benchmark construction. OR-License uses original expert solutions
produced in paid, competitively awarded OR engagements and accepted by
clients before the benchmark was constructed. Hidden evaluation checks
feasibility and compares agent and expert objective quality under the
same instance-specific criteria. The reference anchors evaluation to an
achieved professional outcome, and agents can pursue their own
formulations and solution methods. An agent that produces a feasible
solution with a better objective value receives expert-relative quality
above one.

OR-License combines original industrial materials, client fact
elicitation throughout optimization, and reference deliveries accepted
before benchmark construction, supporting evaluation of the complete
path from understanding an unfamiliar business setting to producing an
executable, feasible, and competitively optimized decision.

## Appendix G Dataset Details

### G.1 Expert Recruitment and Task Construction

##### Expert recruitment.

We recruited contributors with substantial professional operations
research experience to provide source projects and curate them into
benchmark instances. Each expert held a master’s degree or higher in
industrial engineering and operations research, computer science,
electrical engineering, or data science, and had at least three years of
professional OR experience. Experts were compensated at rates
commensurate with their time commitment and level of expertise.

##### Project selection and de-identification.

We selected representative projects from professional OR practice. For
each project, domain experts de-identified the original requirements,
data, and deliverable materials and prepared a brief.md file containing
the business background disclosed to the agent at the start of
evaluation. The agent-facing package retains the associated
de-identified input files. Experts also annotated the client-held
information that could be acquired through ORSim during formulation,
solving, and refinement. The initial brief, input files, and authorized
client disclosures therefore define the information available to the
agent during an episode.

##### Evaluation artifacts and reference solutions.

For each instance, experts supplied hidden constraint-checking verifiers
and objective-function specifications. These artifacts reconstruct the
task-specific operational requirements and remain unavailable to the
agent during execution. We retained the original expert solution and the
original client requirements as source materials for construction and
validation. The reference solutions were produced in commissioned,
competitively awarded OR engagements and accepted by the clients before
benchmark construction. Further checks of the executable reference code,
hidden evaluators, and preserved information boundary are described in
the next subsection.

##### Coverage and source engagements.

The resulting dataset contains 31 instances spanning 10 industrial
scenarios. All source materials were cleared for benchmark use and were
preserved after de-identification without recasting the requirements as
complete mathematical formulations. The source engagements represent
\$3.68 million in total project value, with an average duration of 4.7
months and 2.16 experts per project. Problem-size estimates are reported
in
Appendix [G.3](#A7.SS3 "G.3 Problem Sizes ‣ Appendix G Dataset Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners").

### G.2 Task Quality Control

Experts independently reviewed each instance. They verified that the
human-authored solution code executed correctly and that the hidden
constraint checker and objective function implemented the original
business rules and evaluation criteria. They compared the initial brief
and input files with the original project records to confirm that
de-identification preserved the original information boundaries,
ambiguity, and business terminology. The initial brief retained the
business requirements without recasting them as a complete mathematical
formulation. It excluded facts that required client interaction, which
remained accessible through ORSim, as well as structural insights and
other knowledge acquired during subsequent expert analysis.

### G.4 Verification, Evaluation, and Competency Coverage

Each benchmark instance is evaluated in two logically separate stages.
The *verifier* is a hard feasibility gate: it parses the submitted
artifact, checks the output contract, and recomputes all
constraint-relevant quantities from the canonical input. The *evaluator*
is an independent objective calculator: it independently recomputes the
reported objective, cost, service level, or profit from the submitted
decisions and canonical input.

The following six non-exclusive competency labels summarize task demands
and are not used in scoring:

$`K1`$
direct/static optimization: the business objective and a mostly fixed
mathematical model are explicit;

$`K2`$
objective, model, or policy design: the solver must design proxy
objectives, decomposition/column-generation methods, heuristics, policy
parameters, or rolling decisions when soft preferences, implicit
objectives, or computational scale leave the solution approach
unspecified;

$`K3`$
data analysis and statistical calibration: demand, risk, or scenario
parameters must be estimated from data;

$`K4`$
multi-period or sequential modeling, including batching, sequencing, or
rolling execution;

$`K5`$
multi-scenario or uncertainty modeling;

$`K6`$
secondary criteria and lexicographic/tie-aware reasoning, where equal or
near-equal primary solutions must be distinguished by an additional
criterion.

Table [10](#A7.T10 "Table 10 ‣ G.4 Verification, Evaluation, and Competency Coverage ‣ Appendix G Dataset Details ‣ OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-WorldOperations Research Practitioners")
summarizes the checks, objectives, and competency labels for each task.
Scoring follows the verifier and evaluator versions used in the reported
experiments.

Table 10: Verifier, evaluator, and competency coverage for the 31
benchmark tasks.

The matrix also clarifies the intended separation between business
understanding and mathematical sophistication. Tasks 9–12, 14–19, and 25
are primarily static or directly scored optimization problems: the
central challenge is both translating the business contract into a
feasible model and choosing a solution method suited to the problem
structure. Tasks 14–16 in particular exercise both modeling and solving
for network optimization, while Task 19 also requires choosing a
suitable modeling and solution approach for its combinatorial structure.
Tasks 1, 4, 6–8, 13, and 20–24 require the solver to make modeling or
policy choices that are only partially specified by the surface
objective, especially when soft preferences, rolling execution, or as-of
information boundaries are present. Task 13 and tasks 20–22 additionally
require empirical/statistical analysis of historical data. Tasks 26–31
isolate scenario construction and risk preference (average, recourse,
chance, CVaR, distributional robustness, and finite-scenario
robustness), while also requiring the solver to preserve primary
feasibility and reason about secondary or tie-aware criteria.
